item.title: Noetix’s RMB9,998 Humanoid Is Just the Start
item.dc:creator: TechNode Staff
item.description: Editor’s note: This article is republished from Jumpstart, a TechNode Group publication. item.content:encoded:
Editor’s note: This article is republished from Jumpstart, a TechNode Group publication.

For RMB9,998, Noetix Robotics offered buyers something that had usually belonged to research laboratories, corporate demonstrations and expensive technology showcases: a humanoid robot they could consider buying for themselves.

Bumi, the small robot the Chinese company introduced in October 2025, was aimed at programming education and companionship. Its appeal rested on an immediate proposition. Children could programme its movements, watch it dance and interact with a machine that looked and moved like a small person.

That proposition also expressed a larger choice about how to build a robotics company. Noetix would first make the body affordable and capable enough to sell. More sophisticated intelligence would follow.

Three years after its founding, the company is attempting to turn that sequence into a much larger business. It is pursuing higher deliveries, investing in its own embodied-intelligence models and seeking customers overseas. In October, media reports said it had confidentially submitted a Hong Kong listing application, potentially targeting a 2027 flotation.

The question connecting those ambitions is whether the hardware business Noetix built first can provide enough customers, experience and cash to support what comes next.

A Price Decided Before Production

Founder Jiang Zheyuan left his doctoral studies at Tsinghua University in 2023 and established Noetix that September. His early technical priority was the robot’s body and motion control: the machinery and software that allow it to balance, move and respond reliably.

The distinction matters. A robot can execute demanding movements while relying on external models for conversation or higher-level instructions. Building an athletic machine and building one that can work out what to do in an unfamiliar room involve different capabilities.

Jiang’s decision was to address the physical machine first. He explained that, when the company began, he saw unreliable bodies and limited manufacturing readiness as the immediate bottlenecks. AI approaches were also changing rapidly. Noetix concentrated its resources on hardware while waiting for a clearer direction in the intelligence stack.

Low cost was part of that engineering brief. In a March interview, Jiang described using composite materials in Bumi’s body to reduce its dependence on metal structures. The price was being worked into the design, rather than left for a sales team to negotiate after production.

That approach gave the company a product with a readily understood purpose. Parents and schools could buy a programmable humanoid for education and interaction. They did not have to wait for general-purpose domestic labour to become commercially viable.

The narrower use case helped Noetix reach buyers sooner. It also established the next commercial task: giving those buyers enough continuing value to make the robot more than an exciting first purchase.

Attention Becomes a Manufacturing Problem

Noetix’s machines found a powerful route to public attention through performance. Its N2 robot finished second in the 2025 Beijing humanoid half-marathon. In 2026, the company’s robots appeared alongside comedian Cai Ming in a sketch on China’s Spring Festival Gala.

The exposure connected technical demonstrations with a mass audience. A robot that families had seen on television was also available through retail channels.

At the AWE exhibition in March, Jiang said orders had surged after the gala and set a target of more than 10,000 Bumi sales during 2026. The company was moving from proving that people would notice its robots to showing that it could deliver them consistently.

Jiang’s account of the obstacles was strikingly practical. He identified component availability and production-line management as central challenges. A missing part can stop an entire machine from being completed. As monthly output rises, the company must train and manage a larger workforce while maintaining assembly quality.

These are consequential problems for a company whose market entry depends on affordability. Every reworked unit, delayed delivery and service visit consumes part of the margin that a low selling price leaves available.

The manufacturing target therefore carries more meaning than a shipment milestone. It tests whether Noetix can preserve the economics designed into Bumi while producing and supporting it in much larger numbers.

The Brain Becomes the Expensive Part

By September, Noetix was making its next technical commitment explicit. It launched the embodied-intelligence sub-brand Scalabot and the HERON world-model architecture, extending its ambitions into how robots understand environments and learn to act within them.

The company had begun assembling a dedicated intelligence team in July 2025, according to Jiang’s September interview with Caijing. The work added a substantial research programme to an organisation already scaling physical production.

His logic connects the two activities. Cheaper, reliable machines can be deployed more widely; those deployments can create opportunities to collect experience for training better models.

Making that connection productive requires another layer of engineering. A robot in a classroom generates experience, but useful training data must still be selected, recorded, organised and connected to tasks the company wants its models to learn. A large installed base creates access to potential data. The collection and training system determines its value.

Jiang told 21st Century Business Herald that intelligence research had become a major area of expenditure. He also described hardware as a potential source of funds for that work.

This is the financial hinge in Noetix’s strategy. The body-first approach opened an earlier route to revenue. The company now wants that operating business to help support a more expensive effort whose commercial returns will take longer to develop.

External capital helps bridge the timing. Its backers include Chendao Capital, an investment platform associated with CATL. A prospective Hong Kong listing would take that financing journey into public markets, where investors would be able to examine more closely how hardware sales and research spending fit together.

Taking a Chinese Starting Point Overseas

Noetix’s domestic route has combined educational demand, accessible hardware and unusually broad public exposure. Its overseas expansion will test how much of that combination travels.

At CES in January, co-founder Zhang Shipu outlined five target regions: North America, Europe, the Middle East, Southeast Asia, and Japan and South Korea. He described an ambition to reach thousand-unit scale in overseas expansion during the second quarter, supported by local deployments, customer service and repeatable reference projects.

That programme involves more than shipping robots abroad. Schools need teaching materials and support. Distributors need spare parts and repair arrangements. Families need a reason to keep using the product after its novelty fades.

Noetix has some of those relationships to build from in China. An investor, Beijing Industrial Development Investment Management, reported partnerships with programming-education provider Codemao and retailer Kidswant, alongside deployments and donations involving schools. These connections show how a robot can become part of an existing educational or retail system.

Overseas growth will require comparable connections in markets with different curricula, languages and purchasing habits. The product’s price can win attention, but local usefulness and support will determine whether that attention becomes a durable business.

Noetix’s first move was to make a humanoid affordable enough to enter more classrooms and homes. That choice has given it a product to sell while the broader intelligence problem remains under development.

It is now trying to make that early foothold carry three ambitions at once: larger production volumes, more capable intelligence and international growth. Building the body first won Noetix a place in the market. The next stage is to make that place valuable enough to finance everything it still wants the robot to become.

item.title: How Bambu Lab Turned 3D Printing Into a Consumer Hit
item.dc:creator: Lucia
item.description: Editor’s Note: In 2025, Shenzhen-based Bambu Lab ranked No. 1 globally in shipments of sub-US$2,500 3D printers, with a 37% share, and reportedly surpassed RMB 10 billion in annual revenue. item.content:encoded:
Editor’s Note: In 2025, Shenzhen-based Bambu Lab ranked No. 1 globally in shipments of sub-US$2,500 3D printers, with a 37% share, and reportedly surpassed RMB 10 billion in annual revenue. Its MakerWorld platform reached roughly 10 million monthly active users. Backed by IDG Capital, Temasek, True Light, 5Y Capital, and Mingshi Investment, it combines printers, materials, software, and MakerWorld. And its R1 laser cutter extends that ecosystem into personal manufacturing.

A Shenzhen Company With a Global First Act

In 2022, Bambu Lab took an unusual route to market. Instead of debuting at a domestic trade fair, the young Chinese company launched its first major product, the X1 series, on Kickstarter. The campaign drew 5,575 backers and raised RMB 47.28 million, introducing its former DJI team to a global community of early users.

Afterward, Bambu Lab raised angel backing from Mingshi Investment in 2021, a RMB 30 million Series A from IDG Capital in 2022, a 2023 Series B involving Mingshi, 5Y Capital, Temasek, and True Light Capital, and a RMB 150 million Series C from IDG in April 2024.

Built from the start for global customers, Bambu Lab was founded in Shenzhen in 2020. It operates R&D centers in Shenzhen and Shanghai, with an office in Austin, Texas. Bambu Lab is a Chinese company built from the start for global customers.

For years, desktop 3D printing carried a frustrating contradiction: it promised creative freedom but often required users to become repair technicians. Machines needed leveling, tuning, maintenance, and patience. The X1’s real proposition was not that it made 3D printing new; it made it less exhausting.

With automated calibration, cameras, lidar-assisted monitoring, and its Automatic Material System for multicolor printing, Bambu Lab packaged considerable engineering into something closer to an appliance. Its breakthrough was technical, but also psychological: it reduced the anxiety of pressing print and wondering what would fail.

Overseas First, Ecosystem Next

That approach resonated overseas. Makers, educators, small studios, Etsy sellers, and print-farm operators already knew 3D printing’s potential—and its everyday frustrations: calibration, failed prints, material changes, and maintenance.

Bambu Lab’s answer has been to build an ecosystem around the machine. It sells printers alongside software, branded filaments, accessories, the Bambu Handy app, and MakerWorld, its model-sharing platform. Together, these tools reduce the friction between finding a design and producing a successful print.

For buyers, that ecosystem matters. Without dependable profiles, usable models, compatible materials, or a community, a printer can quickly become an underused machine.

By the end of 2025, MakerWorld had reached about 10 million monthly active users, with an 83% one-year retention rate. The strategy extends Bambu Lab’s role beyond hardware into the broader 3D-printing workflow.

China, meanwhile, is becoming a stronger second engine. By June 2026, Bambu Lab’s cumulative domestic consumer-printer sales had surpassed one million units, while the company reported 2025 revenue above RMB 10 billion.

From Cult Machine to Category Leader

By late 2025, Bambu Lab had moved to the front of the entry-level market. CONTEXT’s Q4 data put it first globally in shipments of 3D printers priced below US$2,500, with a 37% share. That does not make it the leader in industrial 3D printing, but it is a notable result in a field that includes Creality, Elegoo, and Anycubic.

The company has expanded its X1 halo into a layered portfolio. The newer P2S represents the practical middle: a productive machine for serious hobbyists and small businesses, with AI error detection, upgraded airflow, and a quick-swap nozzle system.

At the ambitious end is the H2C. Its Vortek system uses up to six interchangeable hotends and supports as many as 24 filaments, reducing the material waste normally associated with frequent color changes. The H2D Pro reaches toward enterprise users with high-temperature materials, a 350°C nozzle, and an actively heated chamber.

Together, these machines show a company trying to stretch upward without abandoning the users who made it famous: people who want industrial capability without an industrial learning curve.

Scale has also brought legal scrutiny. In September 2026, a Texas jury awarded Stratasys US$27.6 million after finding Bambu Lab liable for infringing four patents; the company plans to seek review and appeal. A European court had earlier declined an injunction in a related case, and the wider dispute remains unresolved.

Beyond the Printer

Having broadened its range within 3D printing, Bambu Lab is now moving into adjacent forms of desktop fabrication. In September 2026, it introduced the R1, a 55W CO₂ laser cutter and engraver—its first dedicated product line beyond 3D printing.

Designed for materials including wood, acrylic, leather, paper, and fabric, the R1 extends the company’s reach from additive manufacturing into cutting and engraving.

The move is logical: a maker who prints a plastic enclosure may also want to cut an acrylic panel or engrave a logo using the same ecosystem. Bambu Lab is thus broadening from 3D printers into a wider range of desktop manufacturing tools.

DragonLab cuts through the noise to find the Chinese startups, founders, and technologies that could shape what comes next.

item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Hangzhou-based AI inference chip developer Nano-core Chip has raised more than RMB 1 billion in Series C2 funding, the company announced on October 28. The round was led by JianTou Investment, with participation from Hangzhou Capital, Kaitai Capital, and other investors. The company will use the proceeds for product development and preparation for volume production. […]
item.content:encoded:
Hangzhou-based AI inference chip developer Nano-core Chip has raised more than RMB 1 billion in Series C2 funding, the company announced on October 28. The round was led by JianTou Investment, with participation from Hangzhou Capital, Kaitai Capital, and other investors.

The company will use the proceeds for product development and preparation for volume production. Founded in 2021 and incubated at a Peking University research institute in Zhejiang, it develops chips that combine three-dimensional near-memory computing, in-memory computing, and RISC-V processing.

Its product lineup targets both devices and cloud infrastructure. The company said its first three chips had completed tape-out, with customer sampling and initial volume shipments planned for early 2027. The latest financing follows a RMB 1 billion Series C1 round announced in September. [Zhidx, in Chinese]

item.title: Former Xiaomi executive launches smart ring and AI-powered sleep system
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: ISHO, the sleep technology startup founded by former Xiaomi executive Wang Teng, unveiled its first products on October 29: the ISHO Ring smart ring and the iFlow bed temperature-control system. Prices start at RMB 1,799 and RMB 9,999, respectively. The ring monitors physiological signals to track sleep and provide daily energy-management insights. It offers a […]
item.content:encoded:
ISHO, the sleep technology startup founded by former Xiaomi executive Wang Teng, unveiled its first products on October 29: the ISHO Ring smart ring and the iFlow bed temperature-control system. Prices start at RMB 1,799 and RMB 9,999, respectively.

The ring monitors physiological signals to track sleep and provide daily energy-management insights. It offers a stated battery life of six to ten days and can store seven days of data offline. The RMB 2,199 Pro package adds an environmental sensing charging case.

The iFlow system combines overnight heart-rate and breathing monitoring with active temperature adjustment, including separate temperature zones for two people sharing a bed. Both products are available for preorder. Ring deliveries are scheduled to begin on November 11, with the standard iFlow system following in December. [Caizhongshe, in Chinese]

item.title: Kai-Fu Lee’s 01.AI secures Hangzhou state investment worth hundreds of millions of RMB
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: 01.AI, the artificial intelligence company founded by Kai-Fu Lee, has secured investment totaling hundreds of millions of RMB from state-backed investors in Hangzhou and the city’s Linping district. The company announced the agreement on October 30, following its signing two days earlier. Under the arrangement, 01.AI will establish its headquarters in Linping and build a […]
item.content:encoded:
01.AI, the artificial intelligence company founded by Kai-Fu Lee, has secured investment totaling hundreds of millions of RMB from state-backed investors in Hangzhou and the city’s Linping district. The company announced the agreement on October 30, following its signing two days earlier.

Under the arrangement, 01.AI will establish its headquarters in Linping and build a base for helping businesses adopt AI. The investment supports its growing focus on enterprise applications and industry-specific AI systems.

The company has been shifting away from consumer-facing services toward enterprise AI solutions. Its public model platform stopped providing model trials and API services in September. Lee has said the company now customizes Chinese open-weight models, including DeepSeek, Qwen, and GLM, for business customers, with roughly half its revenue coming from outside China. [IT Home, in Chinese]

item.title: Xpeng launches MONA L05 SUV with electric and extended-range versions

item.description: Xpeng launched the MONA L05 on October 29, expanding its lower-priced MONA lineup with its first five-seat SUV. Official list prices start at RMB 144,800, while a limited-time launch offer brings the entry price to RMB 139,800. The model comes in battery-electric and extended-range versions. Electric variants offer up to 635 kilometers of CLTC-rated range, […]
item.content:encoded:
Xpeng launched the MONA L05 on October 29, expanding its lower-priced MONA lineup with its first five-seat SUV. Official list prices start at RMB 144,800, while a limited-time launch offer brings the entry price to RMB 139,800.

The model comes in battery-electric and extended-range versions. Electric variants offer up to 635 kilometers of CLTC-rated range, while the extended-range version offers 310 kilometers of electric range and a combined range of 1,310 kilometers. Xpeng said the vehicle was developed for adaptation to 65 countries and regions.

The SUV uses a vision-based assisted-driving system. Max versions carry one Turing AI chip, while Ultra SE versions use two. Xpeng said the first 5,000 vehicles had already rolled off a dedicated production line, allowing vehicle allocation to begin on launch night. [IT Home, in Chinese]

item.title: Xiaomi to invest RMB 1.7 billion in EV battery maker Sunwoda Mobility
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Xiaomi plans to invest RMB 1.7 billion in Sunwoda Mobility, acquiring a 5.34% stake in the electric vehicle battery maker through its wholly owned investment subsidiary, according to an October 29 filing by parent company Sunwoda Electronic. The transaction will involve subscribing for newly issued capital. Following the investment and a planned board reshuffle, Sunwoda […]
item.content:encoded:
Xiaomi plans to invest RMB 1.7 billion in Sunwoda Mobility, acquiring a 5.34% stake in the electric vehicle battery maker through its wholly owned investment subsidiary, according to an October 29 filing by parent company Sunwoda Electronic.

The transaction will involve subscribing for newly issued capital. Following the investment and a planned board reshuffle, Sunwoda Electronic will hold no more than half of Sunwoda Mobility’s board seats. It will consequently cease to control the battery business and stop consolidating its financial results.

The investment deepens Xiaomi’s relationship with a battery supplier as it expands its automotive business. Sunwoda Mobility was already named a strategic partner in Xiaomi’s Dragon Armor battery program, which the automaker introduced in September. [Sunwoda Electronic filing, in Chinese]

item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: HoYoverse, the global brand of Chinese game developer miHoYo, will launch its life simulation game Petit Planet worldwide on December 4 for PC, iOS, and Android. The company announced the date on October 30, following the game’s final beta test. Petit Planet lets players build and customize their own small planets, with activities including farming, […]
item.content:encoded:
HoYoverse, the global brand of Chinese game developer miHoYo, will launch its life simulation game Petit Planet worldwide on December 4 for PC, iOS, and Android. The company announced the date on October 30, following the game’s final beta test.

Petit Planet lets players build and customize their own small planets, with activities including farming, fishing, cooking, and decorating. Players can also explore other planets and meet friends at the Galactic Bazaar. The game supports account progress across its PC and mobile versions.

The title expands the developer’s lineup beyond the combat-focused games that established its international audience, including Genshin Impact, Honkai: Star Rail, and Zenless Zone Zero. A pre-launch special program is scheduled for November 1. [HoYoverse]

item.title: Tencent’s WorkBuddy adds remote control, letting users manage AI tasks from their phones
item.dc:creator: Jessie Wu
item.description: On Thursday, WorkBuddy, Tencent’s AI agent platform, launched a remote control feature supported by Tencent’s Edge One team. The feature allows users to connect to a computer logged into the same account via the mobile app, view the desktop in real time, and take control of operations when necessary. Unlike traditional remote desktop tools, which […]
item.content:encoded:
On Thursday, WorkBuddy, Tencent’s AI agent platform, launched a remote control feature supported by Tencent’s Edge One team. The feature allows users to connect to a computer logged into the same account via the mobile app, view the desktop in real time, and take control of operations when necessary.

Unlike traditional remote desktop tools, which primarily focus on remote access between devices, WorkBuddy’s new feature is designed specifically for AI agent workflows. Users can monitor an agent’s actions in real time and intervene when tasks go off track or require manual authorization.

To use the feature, users need to update the mobile app to version 2.7.0 or later and the macOS desktop client to version 5.9.3 or later. Once connected, the computer screen appears in a floating window on the app’s home page or at the top of a conversation. Users can monitor the agent without leaving the current chat.

If an agent encounters a problem while executing a task, users can intervene directly from their phones. For example, if an account is not logged in or a connector’s authorization has expired, users can try to resolve the issue on their mobile devices rather than returning to their computers.

For manual control, users can tap the full-screen button, which switches the phone interface to landscape mode and enables them to operate the desktop via touch.

The interface provides three options: Controls, Keyboard, and Mouse, which support actions such as switching windows, returning to the desktop, and entering text. A virtual mouse is also available for more precise clicking and scrolling in smaller areas of the screen.

On security, Tencent says the feature limits each computer to one authenticated mobile device at a time. Screen data and control commands are transmitted through an encrypted channel.

The platform does not record user input or store screen footage from remote control sessions. Network traffic generated by remote control is charged against the device’s data usage and does not consume WorkBuddy’s AI agent token quota.

To get started, users must enable the remote connection option for devices logged into the same account in WorkBuddy’s settings, install the required remote control component, and grant screen recording and accessibility permissions. Once configured, users can connect remotely as long as the computer remains powered on and WorkBuddy is online.

In practical terms, the feature helps solve a common challenge in AI agent workflows: the need for human intervention during task execution. AI agents can already handle multi-step tasks such as organizing documents and compiling data, but they may still encounter login requirements, permission requests, or operational errors.

Remote control allows users to monitor progress and make adjustments from their phones without having to stay at their desks.

However, the feature may offer more than just a way for users to operate computers from their phones. It could introduce a more flexible model of human-AI collaboration, with AI handling repetitive work while users step in to make decisions and correct mistakes at critical points.

Rather than pursuing fully autonomous execution at all costs, retaining human oversight may be a more practical approach for AI productivity tools at their current stage of development.

That said, a smartphone cannot fully replicate the experience of working on a computer. Remote access may be convenient for simple tasks such as approving permissions or switching windows, but its efficiency in more complex workflows involving data processing and multiple windows remains to be tested.

The feature is now available for trial to all users. Tencent says future versions will introduce more enterprise-focused capabilities, including tiered permission management and audit logs.

item.title: Phantom Blade Zero Puts Chinese Wuxia Swordplay on a 66-Day Timer
item.dc:creator: Lucia
item.description: An 88 Metascore and 91 OpenCritic average have put S-Game’s dark martial-arts RPG in the conversation as China’s next potential global breakout. Phantom Blade Zero, Chinese developer S-Game’s new wuxia action RPG, launches today on PC and PlayStation 5. The game opens with its protagonist, Soul, impaled through the chest. He chooses an artificial heart […]
item.content:encoded:
An 88 Metascore and 91 OpenCritic average have put S-Game’s dark martial-arts RPG in the conversation as China’s next potential global breakout.

Phantom Blade Zero, Chinese developer S-Game’s new wuxia action RPG, launches today on PC and PlayStation 5. The game opens with its protagonist, Soul, impaled through the chest. He chooses an artificial heart that preserves his emotions—but leaves him only 66 days to live.

That deadline sends him in search of a cure, the truth behind a wider conspiracy, and proof that he did not murder his master. Built in Unreal Engine 5, the game unfolds across the Wulin, its dark and fantastical martial-arts world.

Wuxia, With Steel, Ghosts, and Punk Machinery

For unfamiliar players, wuxia is more than “Chinese sword fighting.” It is a tradition of roaming martial artists, moral debts, revenge, impossible physical skill, and a society outside ordinary law.

Phantom Blade Zero leans into that cinematic language: rain-soaked duels, airborne strikes, rival masters, haunted landscapes, and a hero caught between loyalty and vengeance.

But S-Game gives the tradition a harsher, stranger silhouette. The studio calls its blend of classic martial arts, folk horror, fantasy, and mechanical prosthetics “Kungfupunk.”

The result looks less like historical reconstruction than a stylized martial-arts fever dream—one where a swordsman may face masked assassins, supernatural threats, or machines grafted onto human bodies.

Fast Combat, Not Just Hard Combat

The game’s appeal is likely to rest on its action. Soul can collect more than 30 main weapons and a wide set of secondary “Phantom Edges,” with upgrades, accessories, summons, dodges, counters, and weapon-switching encouraging different builds.

Side quests can open new story routes, while several difficulty settings aim to make the experience accessible beyond the most demanding action-game audience.

Hong Kong kung fu star Donnie Yen, known internationally for the Ip Man films, Rogue One: A Star Wars Story, and John Wick: Chapter 4, served as creative consultant and performed facial and motion capture for Mó Yuan, Soul’s father.

That distinction matters. Though its bosses and checkpoints invite comparisons to Soulslikes, reviews published before launch, including those from GamesRadar and Game Informer, describe a more direct, combo-driven game with adjustable challenge rather than one built around repeated punishment.

Could This Be China’s Next Global Breakout?

The international response before launch has been emphatic. Phantom Blade Zero opened with an 88 Metacritic average and a 91 OpenCritic average. Game Informer awarded it 9.5/10, praising its combat and wuxia scale, while also judging the story less convincing.

TechRadar likewise highlighted the action and atmosphere but noted that its fragmented, terminology-heavy narrative can be difficult to follow.

Although strong reviews alone do not make a Black Myth: Wukong-scale hit, Phantom Blade Zero’s distinctive wuxia world and polished action give it a credible shot at becoming China’s next global breakout.
